title: Recommendations for Secure Use of Transport Layer Security (TLS) and Datagram Transport Layer Security (DTLS)
summary: Gives practical recommendations for configuring and using TLS and DTLS securely, written after several serious attacks on these protocols and their common cipher suites came to light. It covers protocol versions, cipher choices and related settings that help avoid known weaknesses. It was replaced by RFC 9325.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 7525 gives minimum recommendations for configuring TLS and DTLS to protect application traffic. It covers protocol versions, cryptographic choices and several connection settings.

subtitle: RFC 7525's recommendations for using TLS and DTLS securely.

tldr.problem: Attacks had affected TLS and commonly used cipher suites, so implementers and operators needed guidance for protecting application traffic.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC recommends minimum settings for protocol versions, cipher suites, key sizes, session tickets, compression and related TLS features.
tldr.outcome: RFC 7525 is a point-in-time Best Current Practice. It has been obsoleted by RFC 9325 and updated by RFC 8996.

today: RFC 7525 is a Best Current Practice that has been obsoleted by RFC 9325. It was updated by RFC 8996.

sections.title: Why the RFC Gives Recommendations
sections.content:
The document responds to serious attacks on TLS, including attacks on AES-CBC and RC4. Its guidance is a minimum floor for most deployments, not a limit on stronger choices.

The authors describe security best practices as a point-in-time statement because knowledge about attacks and cryptographic strength can change. Unless a recommendation says otherwise, it applies to TLS and DTLS.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC responds to attacks against TLS and older cipher choices. It offers a minimum baseline, and says stronger protections can also be used.

sections.title: Protocol Versions and Connection Settings
sections.content:
Implementations must not negotiate SSL 2 or SSL 3. They must support and prefer TLS 1.2, and should avoid TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1 unless no higher version is available. For DTLS, the document says to support and prefer DTLS 1.2.

The RFC also recommends strict TLS rather than upgrading an initially unencrypted connection where possible. It advises disabling TLS-level compression and protecting and regularly changing session-ticket keys.
sections.plainLanguage: The document tells implementations which older versions not to use and which version to prefer. It also recommends settings that reduce risks during connection setup and session resumption.

sections.title: Cipher Suites and Key Lengths
sections.content:
Implementations must not negotiate NULL-encryption or RC4 suites, or suites offering less than 112 bits of security. They should avoid suites below 128 bits and static RSA key transport, and must support and prefer suites that provide forward secrecy.

The RFC recommends four TLS 1.2 authenticated-encryption suites using DHE or ECDHE with AES-GCM. It recommends Diffie-Hellman keys of at least 2048 bits and RSA certificate moduli of at least 2048 bits.
sections.plainLanguage: A cipher suite sets the cryptographic methods used by a connection. The RFC rules out several weak choices and favors suites that use temporary key agreement.

sections.title: Where the Guidance Applies
sections.content:
The recommendations target common uses of TLS and DTLS for web, email, instant messaging and real-time media. They assume the deployment seeks confidentiality, data integrity and authentication.

The RFC does not change cipher requirements set by existing application protocols. It also excludes opportunistic security cases where following the recommendations might cause a connection to fall back to cleartext.
sections.plainLanguage: The guidance is for connections that need privacy, integrity and authentication. Existing application protocols may have their own requirements that need separate updates.

sections.title: Identity and Forward Secrecy
sections.content:
Applications need to check that a certificate identifies the intended host. The RFC notes that some TLS implementations do not perform host-name validation, so application authors may need to provide it.

Forward secrecy limits the effect of a later compromise of long-term keys on recorded sessions. The RFC also discusses the limits of certificate-revocation checks and recommends that servers support specified OCSP-related mechanisms.
sections.plainLanguage: Encryption alone does not show that a connection reached the intended server; identity checks matter too. Forward secrecy can limit what an attacker learns from long-term keys obtained later.
